Statement I: If two systems A and B are each separately in thermal equilibrium with a third system C, then A and B need not be in thermal equilibrium with each other.
Statement II: A body contains a definite amount of heat, so heat is a thermodynamic state variable like temperature.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Zeroth law, and heat as energy in transit
solution.explanation: The zeroth law says the opposite of Statement I: A and B must be in thermal equilibrium with each other, which is what allows temperature to be defined. Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; a body has internal energy, not 'heat', and the heat exchanged depends on the process, so heat is not a state variable.
steps: Statement I contradicts the zeroth law → false
Statement II: heat is energy in transit, path dependent → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are false: Statement I negates the zeroth law and Statement II confuses heat with internal energy.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', zeroth law; heat, internal energy and work
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A gas is enclosed in a cylinder whose walls and piston are perfectly insulating. The gas is compressed by pushing the piston in. The process is:

options.text: Adiabatic, and the temperature of the gas falls
Adiabatic, and the temperature of the gas rises
Isothermal, and the temperature of the gas stays constant
Isochoric, and the temperature of the gas rises

solution.concept: Adiabatic compression
solution.explanation: Perfectly insulating walls allow no heat exchange, so Q = 0 and the process is adiabatic. The work done on the gas then all goes into its internal energy: ΔU = −W > 0 for a compression, so the temperature rises.
steps: Compression: W (by gas) < 0 → ΔU = −W > 0 → T rises
solution.why_others_wrong: An adiabatic expansion (not compression) cools the gas. An isothermal process needs heat exchange with a reservoir, impossible through insulating walls. The volume changes, so it is not isochoric.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', adiabatic process
solution.final_answer: Option B: Adiabatic, and the temperature of the gas rises

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An ideal gas is taken round the cycle A → B → C → A. From A (1 L, 1 × 10⁵ Pa) it expands at constant pressure to B (3 L, 1 × 10⁵ Pa). It is then compressed to C (1 L, 4 × 10⁵ Pa) along a straight line on the P–V diagram, and finally its pressure is lowered at constant volume back to A. The net heat absorbed by the gas in one cycle is:

options.text: +300 J, i.e. the gas absorbs 300 J of heat
−600 J, i.e. the gas gives out 600 J of heat
−300 J, i.e. the gas gives out 300 J of heat
Zero, since the process is cyclic

solution.concept: First law for a cyclic process
solution.explanation: In a cycle ΔU = 0, so the net heat absorbed equals the net work done by the gas, which is the area enclosed on the P–V diagram, positive for a clockwise cycle and negative for an anticlockwise one. Here the compression B → C happens at higher pressures than the expansion A → B, so more work is done on the gas than by it.
steps: Q_net = W_net = 200 − 500 = −300 J (triangle area ½ × 2 × 10⁻³ × 3 × 10⁵ = 300 J)
solution.why_others_wrong: +300 J has the right size but the wrong sign: the cycle runs anticlockwise. −600 J takes the whole rectangle instead of the triangle. Zero confuses ΔU = 0 with Q = 0.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', first law and cyclic processes
solution.final_answer: Option C: −300 J, i.e. the gas gives out 300 J of heat

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An ideal diatomic gas (γ = 1.4) at 280 K is compressed reversibly and adiabatically until its pressure becomes 128 times its initial pressure. Its final temperature is:

solution.concept: Pressure–temperature relation in an adiabatic process
solution.explanation: Combining PV^γ = constant with PV = nRT gives T ∝ P^((γ−1)/γ) for a reversible adiabatic process.
solution.why_others_wrong: 560 K uses the exponent 1/7. 280 K treats the compression as isothermal. 2240 K uses the exponent 3/7.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', adiabatic process

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When a gas in a cylinder is compressed very rapidly by a piston, its temperature rises.
Reason (R): During a very rapid compression, heat flows into the gas from the surroundings.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Rapid processes are nearly adiabatic
solution.explanation: A very rapid compression leaves no time for heat exchange, so it is nearly adiabatic (Q ≈ 0). The work done on the gas then raises its internal energy, and so its temperature (the reason a bicycle pump gets hot). Heat does not flow in; if anything, the warmed gas would later lose heat to the surroundings.
steps: Rapid → Q ≈ 0 → ΔU = work done on gas > 0 → T rises → A true
No time for heat flow, and the gas becomes hotter than the surroundings → R false
solution.why_others_wrong: R gives a wrong mechanism: the temperature rises because of the work done on the gas, not because of heat flowing in.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', adiabatic process
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A fixed amount of an ideal gas undergoes each of the processes in List-I. Q is the heat absorbed by the gas, W the work done by the gas and ΔU the change in its internal energy. Match List-I with List-II.

List-I:
A. Isothermal expansion
B. Adiabatic expansion
C. Heating at constant volume
D. Compression at constant pressure

List-II:
I. Q = 0 and ΔU < 0
II. W = 0 and ΔU > 0
III. Q > 0 and ΔU = 0
IV. Q < 0, W < 0 and ΔU < 0

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Signs of Q, W and ΔU in ideal-gas processes
solution.explanation: Apply Q = ΔU + W, remembering that ΔU of an ideal gas follows its temperature, and that W > 0 for expansion. In an isobaric compression V falls at constant P, so T = PV/nR falls too.
steps: Isothermal expansion: ΔU = 0, W > 0 → Q > 0 → III
Adiabatic expansion: Q = 0, W > 0 → ΔU < 0 → I
Isochoric heating: W = 0, T rises → ΔU > 0 → II
Isobaric compression: W < 0, T falls → ΔU < 0 → Q = ΔU + W < 0 → IV
solution.why_others_wrong: The wrong codes swap the isothermal and adiabatic expansions, or think an isobaric compression warms the gas.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', first law and thermodynamic processes
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-I, C-II, D-IV

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Equal amounts of the same ideal gas, starting from the same initial state, are expanded reversibly from volume V to volume 2V in three different ways: (i) at constant pressure, (ii) isothermally and (iii) adiabatically. If W₁, W₂ and W₃ are the respective works done by the gas, then:

solution.concept: Comparing works from P–V curves
solution.explanation: The work done is the area under the P–V curve from V to 2V. From the same starting point, the isobaric line is horizontal, the isotherm falls (P ∝ 1/V), and the adiabat falls even more steeply (P ∝ 1/V^γ). So the areas, and the works, are in the order isobaric > isothermal > adiabatic.
solution.why_others_wrong: W₃ > W₂ > W₁ reverses the order. W₂ > W₁ forgets that pressure stays highest in the isobaric process. Equal works ignore that work depends on the path.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', isothermal and adiabatic processes

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A gas is taken from state A to state B along path 1, absorbing 80 J of heat and doing 50 J of work. It is then brought back from B to A along a different path, during which 40 J of work is done ON the gas. In the return from B to A, the gas:

solution.concept: Internal energy as a state function
solution.explanation: ΔU between two states is the same for every path. Find U_B − U_A from path 1, then apply the first law to the return path with the correct signs.
steps: Return: ΔU_BA = −30 J, W_BA = −40 J (work done on the gas)
Q_BA = ΔU_BA + W_BA = −30 − 40 = −70 J → 70 J given out
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Absorbs 10 J' and 'gives out 10 J' add −30 and +40 with a sign error in W. 'Absorbs 70 J' has the right size but the wrong sign.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', first law of thermodynamics
solution.final_answer: Option B: Gives out 70 J of heat

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Two identical samples of an ideal gas start from the same state. One is compressed reversibly and isothermally, and the other reversibly and adiabatically, both to the same final volume. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The final pressure is greater in the adiabatic compression.
(b) More work is done on the gas in the adiabatic compression.
(c) In the isothermal compression, the gas gives out heat equal to the work done on it.
(d) In the adiabatic compression, the internal energy of the gas decreases.
(e) The final temperature is the same in both compressions.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Isothermal versus adiabatic compression
solution.explanation: For compression from the same point, the adiabat (PV^γ = constant) rises more steeply than the isotherm (PV = constant), so the pressure is higher at every smaller volume, the final pressure is higher, and the area under the curve (work done on the gas) is larger. In the isothermal case ΔU = 0, so the heat given out equals the work done on the gas. In the adiabatic case Q = 0 and the work done on the gas raises U and T.
steps: (e) adiabatic T rises, isothermal T constant → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Codes with (d) or (e) treat the adiabatic compression as if it cooled the gas or kept T fixed; (a) and (c) only misses (b).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Thermodynamics', isothermal and adiabatic processes

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) For μ moles of an ideal gas, PV = μRT, where R is the universal gas constant.
(b) Boltzmann's constant is related to the gas constant R and Avogadro's number N_A by k_B = N_A/R.
(c) Real gases approach ideal-gas behaviour at low pressures and high temperatures.
(d) The value of the gas constant R is different for different gases.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Ideal gas equation
solution.explanation: The ideal gas equation is PV = μRT with the same R for all gases. Writing μ = N/N_A gives PV = Nk_BT with k_B = R/N_A. Real gases behave nearly ideally when the molecules are far apart and fast (low pressure, high temperature).
solution.why_others_wrong: Codes with (b) invert the relation between k_B, R and N_A; codes with (d) forget that R is universal.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Kinetic Theory', molecular nature of matter and behaviour of gases

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The number of molecules in 22.4 litres of any ideal gas at standard temperature and pressure (273 K, 1 atm) is about:

solution.concept: Avogadro's number
solution.explanation: One mole of an ideal gas occupies 22.4 L at STP, and one mole contains Avogadro's number of molecules, N_A = 6.02 × 10²³. This also follows from Avogadro's hypothesis that equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.69 × 10²⁵ is roughly the number in one cubic metre at STP. 6.02 × 10²⁶ is the number in a kilomole. 1.38 × 10⁻²³ is Boltzmann's constant in J/K.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Kinetic Theory', behaviour of gases (Avogadro's hypothesis)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
One mole of a monatomic ideal gas is at 300 K. Taking R = 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and using the law of equipartition of energy, match List-I (quantity) with List-II (its numerical value in SI units).

List-I:
A. Internal energy of the gas (in J)
B. Molar specific heat at constant volume (in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
C. Molar specific heat at constant pressure (in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹)
D. Product PV of its pressure and volume (in J)

List-II:
I. 2490
II. 20.75
III. 3735
IV. 12.45

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Equipartition and specific heats of a monatomic gas
solution.explanation: A monatomic molecule has 3 translational degrees of freedom, each with ½k_BT on average, so U = (3/2)RT per mole and C_v = (3/2)R. Then C_p = C_v + R = (5/2)R, and PV = RT for one mole.
solution.why_others_wrong: The wrong codes swap U with PV, or C_v with C_p.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Kinetic Theory', law of equipartition of energy and specific heat capacity
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For a gas in equilibrium in a stationary container, the average velocity (a vector) of its molecules is zero, although their rms speed is not zero.
Statement II: The pressure exerted by a mixture of non-reacting ideal gases is the sum of the pressures that each gas would exert if it alone occupied the container at the same temperature.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Molecular velocities and Dalton's law of partial pressures
solution.explanation: Molecular motion is random: for every molecule moving one way there is, on average, another moving the opposite way, so the vector average is zero while the average of v² is not. In kinetic theory each gas in a mixture contributes (1/3)nm⟨v²⟩ independently, so the partial pressures add (Dalton's law).
steps: Statement I: random directions → ⟨v⟩ = 0, but ⟨v²⟩ ≠ 0 → true
Statement II: P = P₁ + P₂ + … → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are standard results of kinetic theory.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Kinetic Theory', pressure of an ideal gas (law of partial pressures)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: One mole of oxygen (rigid diatomic molecules) at 300 K and one mole of helium (monatomic) at 380 K are mixed in a thermally insulated, rigid container. Treating both as ideal gases and using the law of equipartition of energy, the final temperature of the mixture is:

solution.concept: Energy conservation with equipartition specific heats
solution.explanation: No heat enters and no work is done (rigid, insulated container), so the total internal energy is conserved. The internal energy of each gas is μC_vT, with C_v = (5/2)R for rigid diatomic oxygen and (3/2)R for helium.
solution.why_others_wrong: 340 K is the simple average, ignoring the different specific heats. 350 K swaps the specific heats of the two gases. 333 K uses C_p instead of C_v, although the container is rigid.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Kinetic Theory', law of equipartition of energy and specific heats of gases

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Oxygen gas (O₂) at absolute temperature T has an rms molecular speed v. The temperature is raised to 2T, and at this temperature all the molecules dissociate into oxygen atoms. Treating the gas as ideal, the rms speed of the oxygen atoms is:

solution.concept: Dependence of rms speed on temperature and molar mass
solution.explanation: v_rms = √(3RT/M). Doubling T multiplies v_rms by √2; halving the molar mass (O₂ → O, 32 → 16 g/mol) multiplies it by a further √2.
solution.why_others_wrong: √2 v accounts for only one of the two changes. v ignores both. 2√2 v takes the molar mass as falling by a factor of 4.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Kinetic Theory', kinetic interpretation of temperature (rms speed)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A sound wave of frequency 680 Hz travels through air with a speed of 340 m/s. The phase difference between the oscillations of two points of the air, 25 cm apart along the direction of propagation, is:

solution.concept: Phase difference and path difference in a progressive wave
solution.explanation: At a given instant, points separated by Δx along the wave differ in phase by kΔx = 2πΔx/λ.
solution.why_others_wrong: π/2 rad and π/4 rad take the separation as λ/4 or λ/8. 2π rad takes it as a full wavelength.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Waves', displacement relation in a progressive wave (phase)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A block attached to a spring oscillates on a smooth horizontal surface. The amplitude of the oscillation is increased from 2 cm to 6 cm, the block and spring being the same. The total energy of the oscillation becomes:

options.text: Unchanged, since the frequency is unchanged

solution.concept: Energy of a simple harmonic oscillator
solution.explanation: The total energy of a spring–block oscillator is E = ½kA², so with the same spring it is proportional to the square of the amplitude.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 times assumes E ∝ A. 6 times adds instead of squaring. The frequency is indeed unchanged, but the energy depends on the amplitude.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Oscillations', energy in simple harmonic motion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The equation y(x, t) = a sin(kx + ωt), where a, k and ω are positive constants, represents a wave travelling:

options.text: Along the positive x-direction with speed ω/k
Along the negative x-direction with speed k/ω
Along the negative x-direction with speed ω/k
Nowhere: it is a stationary wave

solution.concept: Direction of a travelling wave from its equation
solution.explanation: A fixed phase kx + ωt = constant moves so that x decreases as t increases: dx/dt = −ω/k. So the wave travels along −x with speed ω/k. The form sin(kx − ωt) would travel along +x.
solution.why_others_wrong: The positive direction belongs to sin(kx − ωt). k/ω is the reciprocal of the speed. A stationary wave has a product form such as sin kx cos ωt.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Waves', displacement relation in a progressive wave
solution.final_answer: Option C: Along the negative x-direction with speed ω/k

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When two waves of the same amplitude arrive at a point exactly in opposite phase, the resultant displacement at that point is zero.
Reason (R): According to the principle of superposition, the resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of the displacements due to the individual waves.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Principle of superposition (destructive interference)
solution.explanation: In opposite phase the two displacements at every instant are equal in size and opposite in sign, so their algebraic sum is zero.
steps: y₁ = a sin ωt, y₂ = a sin(ωt + π) = −a sin ωt
solution.why_others_wrong: The zero resultant follows directly from adding the displacements, as R states.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Waves', the principle of superposition of waves
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in its fundamental mode. Its vibrating length is reduced by 20%, the tension and the string being unchanged. Its fundamental frequency:

solution.concept: Fundamental frequency of a stretched string
solution.explanation: In the fundamental mode λ = 2L, so f = v/(2L). With the same tension and mass per unit length, v is unchanged and f ∝ 1/L.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20% assumes f changes by the same percentage as L. A decrease would follow from f ∝ L. 12% uses f ∝ 1/√L.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Waves', standing waves and normal modes of a string

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two sound waves arriving at a point produce displacements y₁ = a sin(400πt) and y₂ = a sin(406πt), where t is in seconds. The number of beats heard per second is:

solution.concept: Beat frequency
solution.explanation: Read each frequency from ω = 2πf. The beat frequency is the difference of the two frequencies, not of the angular frequencies.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 subtracts the coefficients 406 − 400 directly (angular frequency/π). 1.5 halves the beat frequency. 203 Hz is the frequency of the second wave.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Waves', beats

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: At what temperature will the speed of sound in air be twice its value at 0 °C? (Treat air as an ideal gas.)

solution.concept: Variation of the speed of sound with temperature
solution.explanation: For an ideal gas v = √(γRT/M), so v ∝ √T with T in kelvin. Doubling v needs four times the absolute temperature.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1092 °C forgets to convert back from kelvin. 273 °C (546 K) doubles the absolute temperature, which only raises v by √2. 546 °C mixes up the scales.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Waves', speed of a longitudinal wave (Laplace correction)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The motion of a simple pendulum is simple harmonic only for small angular displacements.
Statement II: The period of a simple pendulum of fixed length increases when it is taken from the Earth's surface to the top of a high mountain.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Simple pendulum
solution.explanation: The restoring torque is −mgL sin θ. Only when sin θ ≈ θ (small angles) is it proportional to the displacement, which is the condition for SHM. The period T = 2π√(L/g) increases where g is smaller, and g decreases with height above the surface.
steps: Statement I: sin θ ≈ θ needed → true
Statement II: g decreases with height → T increases → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are correct consequences of T = 2π√(L/g) and its small-angle derivation.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Oscillations', the simple pendulum
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A particle executes simple harmonic motion x = A sin(2πt/T), where T is the period. Match List-I (time t) with List-II (displacement x at that time).

List-I:
A. t = T/12
B. t = T/8
C. t = T/4
D. t = T/2

List-II:
I. Zero
II. A/√2
III. A/2
IV. A

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Displacement and phase in SHM
solution.explanation: The phase at time t is 2πt/T. Evaluate sin of the phase at each time.
steps: T/12: phase π/6 → x = A/2 → III
T/8: phase π/4 → x = A/√2 → II
T/4: phase π/2 → x = A → IV
solution.why_others_wrong: The wrong codes swap T/12 and T/8, or put the extreme position at T/2 instead of T/4.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Oscillations', simple harmonic motion (phase)
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A stationary (standing) wave is set up on a stretched string fixed at both ends. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) Both fixed ends are nodes.
(b) The frequencies of the normal modes are integral multiples of the fundamental frequency.
(c) The distance between two consecutive nodes is half a wavelength.
(d) All the points between two consecutive nodes oscillate with the same amplitude.
(e) In the fundamental mode, the wavelength equals the length of the string.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Normal modes of a string fixed at both ends
solution.explanation: Fixed ends cannot move, so they are nodes. Fitting a whole number of half-wavelengths into L gives λₙ = 2L/n and fₙ = nv/(2L), integral multiples of v/2L. Nodes are λ/2 apart. The amplitude 2a|sin kx| varies from zero at the nodes to a maximum at the antinodes.
solution.why_others_wrong: Codes with (d) treat a standing wave like a travelling wave of uniform amplitude; codes with (e) forget that the fundamental is half a wavelength long.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Waves', standing waves and normal modes

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A block of mass 1.5 kg rests on a smooth horizontal surface, attached to a light horizontal spring of spring constant 400 N/m whose other end is fixed. A ball of putty of mass 0.5 kg moving at 4 m/s along the axis of the spring hits the block and sticks to it. The amplitude of the resulting oscillations is:

solution.concept: SHM after a perfectly inelastic collision
solution.explanation: The collision happens at the equilibrium position, so the common velocity just after it is the maximum velocity of the new oscillation: v_max = Aω, with ω = √(k/(m + M)).
solution.why_others_wrong: 10√2 cm equates the putty's kinetic energy before the collision to ½kA², ignoring the loss in the inelastic collision. 2.5√6 cm uses only the block's mass (1.5 kg) in ω. 2.5√2 cm uses only the putty's mass (0.5 kg) in ω.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Oscillations', oscillations due to a spring

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A string 1.2 m long is fixed at both ends. Two successive resonant frequencies of the string are 300 Hz and 400 Hz, with no resonance between them. The speed of transverse waves on the string is:

solution.concept: Successive harmonics of a string
solution.explanation: The normal-mode frequencies are fₙ = n v/(2L). Successive harmonics differ by the fundamental frequency f₁ = v/(2L).
steps: f₁ = 400 − 300 = 100 Hz (300 Hz and 400 Hz are the 3rd and 4th harmonics)
solution.why_others_wrong: 120 m/s uses v = Lf₁. 480 m/s uses v = 4Lf₁, as for a pipe closed at one end. 960 m/s uses 400 Hz as the fundamental.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Waves', standing waves and normal modes

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A pipe open at both ends has fundamental frequency f. The pipe is now closed at one end, its length being unchanged. The frequency of the third harmonic of the closed pipe is found to be 100 Hz higher than f. Neglecting end corrections, f is:

solution.concept: Harmonics of open and closed pipes
solution.explanation: For length L, an open pipe has fundamental v/(2L). A pipe closed at one end has fundamental v/(4L), i.e. f/2, and only odd harmonics; its third harmonic is 3v/(4L) = 3f/2.
solution.why_others_wrong: 100 Hz takes the closed pipe's third harmonic as 2f. 400 Hz takes it as 5f/4. 300 Hz is the closed pipe's third harmonic itself.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Waves', standing waves in pipes

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): At a constant temperature, the speed of sound in an ideal gas increases when the pressure of the gas is increased.
Reason (R): At a constant temperature, the ratio P/ρ of the pressure to the density of a given ideal gas remains constant.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Effect of pressure on the speed of sound
solution.explanation: v = √(γP/ρ). For an ideal gas P/ρ = RT/M, which depends only on temperature. Raising the pressure at constant temperature raises the density in the same proportion, so the speed does not change.
steps: P = ρRT/M → P/ρ = RT/M (constant at fixed T) → R true
solution.why_others_wrong: A is the trap: pressure appears in Laplace's formula, but density changes with it.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Waves', speed of a longitudinal wave (Laplace correction)
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two point charges kept a certain distance apart in air repel each other with a force of 8 N. Keeping the separation unchanged, they are immersed in an oil of dielectric constant 4. The force between them now is:

solution.concept: Coulomb's law in a dielectric medium
solution.explanation: In a medium of dielectric constant K the permittivity is Kε₀, so the Coulomb force between the same charges at the same separation is reduced by the factor K.
solution.why_others_wrong: 32 N multiplies by K. 4 N divides by √K. 0.5 N divides by K².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', Coulomb's law (permittivity of a medium)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Point charges of +2 μC and −3 μC are held 30 cm apart in air. Taking 1/(4πε₀) = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and the potential energy to be zero at infinite separation, the electrostatic potential energy of the pair is:

solution.concept: Potential energy of a system of two point charges
solution.explanation: U = q₁q₂/(4πε₀r), with the signs of the charges kept. Unlike charges give a negative potential energy.
solution.why_others_wrong: +0.18 J drops the sign of the negative charge. −0.6 J divides by r² (that is the force in newtons, with a sign). −0.054 J forgets to divide by r.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', potential energy of a system of charges

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Capacitors of 2 μF, 3 μF and 6 μF are connected in series. Their equivalent capacitance is:

solution.concept: Capacitors in series
solution.explanation: In series the reciprocals of the capacitances add: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + 1/C₃. The result is smaller than the smallest capacitance.
solution.why_others_wrong: 11 μF is the parallel sum. 2 μF and 0.5 μF do not follow from the series rule (0.5 μF would be 1/C = 2).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', combination of capacitors

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (property or law) with List-II (its statement).

List-I:
A. Additivity of charges
B. Quantisation of charge
C. Conservation of charge
D. Coulomb's law

List-II:
I. The charge on any body is an integral multiple of e, q = ne
II. The total charge of an isolated system remains constant
III. The force between two point charges varies as q₁q₂/r²
IV. The total charge of a system is the algebraic sum of the individual charges

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Basic properties of electric charge
solution.explanation: NCERT lists three basic properties of charge (additivity, conservation and quantisation), and Coulomb's law gives the force between point charges.
solution.why_others_wrong: The wrong codes swap additivity with conservation, or quantisation with additivity.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', basic properties of electric charge
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Which of the following molecules has a permanent electric dipole moment (is a polar molecule)?

solution.concept: Polar and non-polar molecules
solution.explanation: In a polar molecule the centres of positive and negative charge do not coincide even without an external field. NCERT gives water (H₂O) as an example. In CO₂ and CH₄ the centres coincide because of the symmetry of the molecule, and O₂ is a symmetric molecule of two identical atoms; these are non-polar.
steps: H₂O: bent molecule → charge centres separated → polar
solution.why_others_wrong: CO₂ and CH₄ are NCERT's examples of non-polar molecules; O₂ has no charge separation either.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', physical significance of dipoles

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor increases when the separation between its plates is decreased.
Reason (R): The energy stored in a capacitor of capacitance C carrying a charge Q is Q²/(2C).

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor
solution.explanation: C = ε₀A/d, so a smaller separation d gives a larger capacitance; A is true. R is a correct formula for the stored energy, but it is about a different property of the capacitor and says nothing about how C depends on d.
steps: C = ε₀A/d → d decreases → C increases (A true)
U = Q²/2C (R true, but unrelated to A)
solution.why_others_wrong: R does not mention the plate separation at all, so it cannot explain A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', the parallel plate capacitor
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A charge of +4 μC is fixed at x = 0 and a charge of −4 μC at x = 0.2 m on the x-axis, in air. A charge of +1 μC is placed at x = 0.1 m. Taking 1/(4πε₀) = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the net force on the +1 μC charge is:

solution.concept: Superposition of Coulomb forces
solution.explanation: The +4 μC charge repels the +1 μC charge towards +x, and the −4 μC charge attracts it, also towards +x. The two forces are equal in size and in the same direction, so they add.
solution.why_others_wrong: Zero treats the two forces as opposite, as they would be for two like charges. 3.6 N counts only one charge. −x reverses both forces.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', forces between multiple charges

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A tiny oil drop of mass 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg is held stationary in air by a uniform vertical electric field of magnitude 1 × 10⁵ N/C. The drop carries excess electrons. Taking g = 10 m/s², e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and neglecting buoyancy, the number of excess electrons on the drop is:

solution.concept: Balance of electric and gravitational forces; quantisation of charge
solution.explanation: For the drop to stay at rest, the electric force qE must balance its weight mg. (Since the drop is negatively charged, the field must point downward to give an upward force.) The charge is then a whole number of electronic charges.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 and 4 come from slips of a factor of 2 (dropping or doubling e). 20 forgets g = 10 in mg.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', electric field and quantisation of charge

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin spherical conducting shell of radius 20 cm, in air, is charged so that its potential is 3000 V (zero at infinity). The magnitude of the electric field just outside its surface is:

solution.concept: Field and potential of a charged spherical shell
solution.explanation: Outside the shell, by Gauss's law, the field and potential are those of a point charge Q at the centre: E = kQ/r² and V = kQ/r. At the surface (r = R) they are related by E = V/R.
steps: V = kQ/R and E = kQ/R² → E = V/R
solution.why_others_wrong: 600 V/m multiplies V by R. Zero is the field inside the shell, not just outside it. 7.5 × 10⁴ V/m divides by R².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', applications of Gauss's law (thin spherical shell)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A parallel plate capacitor with air between its plates, which are 1 mm apart, is charged to a potential difference of 1000 V. Taking ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻², the energy stored per unit volume in the field between the plates is about:

solution.concept: Energy density of an electric field
solution.explanation: Between the plates the field is uniform, E = V/d, and the energy density is u = ½ε₀E².
solution.why_others_wrong: 8.9 J/m³ drops the ½. 4.4 × 10⁻⁶ J/m³ uses E = 1000 V/m (d in mm). 4.4 × 10⁻³ J/m³ is a powers-of-ten slip in E.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', energy stored in a capacitor (energy density)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A charge of 1 nC is uniformly distributed over a thin ring of radius 0.3 m, in air. Taking 1/(4πε₀) = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and the potential to be zero at infinity, the electric potential at a point on the axis of the ring, 0.4 m from its centre, is:

solution.concept: Potential due to a system of charges
solution.explanation: Potential is a scalar, so the contributions of all the elements of the ring simply add. Every element is at the same distance √(R² + x²) from a point on the axis, so the ring acts like its whole charge at that distance.
solution.why_others_wrong: 22.5 V uses the axial distance 0.4 m. 30 V uses the radius 0.3 m. Zero confuses the potential with the field at the centre of the ring.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', potential due to a system of charges

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When two charged conductors are connected by a conducting wire, charge flows between them until their potentials become equal.
Statement II: When a dielectric slab is placed in a uniform external electric field, equal and opposite surface charges are induced on its two faces.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Conductors in contact; polarisation of a dielectric
solution.explanation: Charges in a conductor move from higher to lower potential energy until the whole connected conductor is at one potential, so the flow stops when the two potentials are equal. A dielectric in a field becomes polarised; inside, the dipoles cancel, leaving surface charge densities +σₚ and −σₚ on the two faces, whose field opposes the external field.
steps: Statement I: flow stops at equal potential → true
Statement II: polarisation → ±σₚ on opposite faces → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both are NCERT descriptions of conductors and dielectrics.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', conductors and dielectrics (polarisation)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match List-I (situation) with List-II (electric flux through the stated surface). The charges are in vacuum.

List-I:
A. A point charge q at the centre of a cube: flux through the whole cube
B. A point charge q at the centre of a cube: flux through one face
C. A point charge q at one corner of a cube: flux through the whole cube
D. An electric dipole lying entirely inside a closed surface: flux through that surface

List-II:
I. q/(6ε₀)
II. Zero
III. q/ε₀
IV. q/(8ε₀)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Gauss's law and symmetry
solution.explanation: The total flux through a closed surface is q_enclosed/ε₀. A charge at the centre of a cube sends equal flux through the six faces. A charge at a corner is shared by eight cubes that meet there, so one cube gets 1/8 of the total. A dipole has zero net charge.
steps: D: net charge 0 → zero flux → II
solution.why_others_wrong: The wrong codes swap the face flux with the corner case, or give a dipole a non-zero flux.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', Gauss's law
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Two capacitors of different capacitances are charged by connecting them to a battery, first in parallel and then, separately, in series. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) In parallel, the charges on the capacitors are in the ratio of their capacitances.
(b) In series, the potential differences across the capacitors are in the inverse ratio of their capacitances.
(c) The equivalent capacitance of the parallel combination is less than the smaller capacitance.
(d) In series, the capacitor of larger capacitance stores more energy.
(e) In parallel, the capacitor of larger capacitance stores more energy.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Charge, voltage and energy in series and parallel combinations
solution.explanation: In parallel the voltage is common, so Q = CV ∝ C and U = ½CV² ∝ C. In series the charge is common, so V = Q/C ∝ 1/C and U = Q²/(2C) ∝ 1/C: the smaller capacitor stores more. The parallel equivalent is the sum, larger than either capacitance.
steps: (d) series: U = Q²/2C → smaller C stores more → false
(e) parallel: U = ½CV² → larger C stores more → true
solution.why_others_wrong: Codes with (d) apply ½CV² to the series case, where V is not common; codes with (c) use the series rule for a parallel combination.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', combination of capacitors and energy stored

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about electrostatic forces and fields are correct?

(a) The force between two point charges is not changed by the presence of a third charge nearby.
(b) The electrostatic force between two point charges acts along the line joining them.
(c) Coulomb's law in its simple form applies to point charges, i.e. charged bodies whose sizes are small compared with the distance between them.
(d) The electric field produced by a point charge at a given point depends on the size of the small test charge used to measure it.
(e) Two unequal point charges exert forces of equal magnitude on each other.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Coulomb's law and the superposition principle
solution.explanation: By the superposition principle, the force between any two charges is unaffected by other charges; the net force on a charge is the vector sum of these pair forces. Coulomb forces are central and obey Newton's third law whatever the sizes of the charges. The field E = F/q is a property of the source charge alone; the test charge only measures it.
steps: (d) E = F/q is independent of q → false
solution.why_others_wrong: (b), (c) and (e) only leaves out the superposition statement (a), which students often doubt; codes with (d) make the field depend on the probe.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', Coulomb's law, forces between multiple charges and electric field

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A 10 μF air-filled parallel plate capacitor remains connected to a 20 V battery. A dielectric slab of dielectric constant 3 is inserted so that it completely fills the space between the plates. The extra charge drawn from the battery and the increase in the energy stored in the capacitor are respectively:

solution.concept: Dielectric inserted at constant potential difference
solution.explanation: With the battery connected, V stays 20 V while C becomes KC₀. The charge and the stored energy (½CV²) both become K times as large. The battery does work (ΔQ)V, twice the increase in stored energy; the rest goes into pulling the slab in.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8 mJ is the work done by the battery, not the increase in stored energy. 'Zero' treats the charge as fixed, which holds only with the battery disconnected. 600 μC and 6 mJ are the final values, not the changes.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', effect of dielectric on capacitance and energy stored

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A point charge of +2 μC is held fixed. A small particle of mass 1 g carrying a charge of +1 μC is projected straight towards it from a very large distance with a speed of 6 m/s. Taking 1/(4πε₀) = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² and neglecting gravity, the distance of closest approach between them is:

solution.concept: Conservation of energy with electrostatic potential energy
solution.explanation: As the particle approaches, its kinetic energy is converted into electrostatic potential energy. At the closest approach it is momentarily at rest, so all its initial kinetic energy has become q₁q₂/(4πε₀r).
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.5 m uses mv² instead of ½mv² for the kinetic energy. 2 m halves the potential energy. 0.1 m is a powers-of-ten slip.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', potential energy of a system of charges

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Four point charges are placed at the corners of a square ABCD of side 0.3 m, in air: +1 μC at A and at B, and −1 μC at C and at D (A, B, C, D taken in order round the square). Taking 1/(4πε₀) = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², the magnitude of the electric field at the centre of the square is:

solution.concept: Superposition of electric fields
solution.explanation: Each charge is at a distance a/√2 from the centre and produces a field kq/(a²/2) = 2kq/a². Opposite corners carry opposite charges, so along each diagonal the two fields point the same way and add. The two diagonal resultants are perpendicular.
steps: Along diagonal AC: 2 × 2 × 10⁵ = 4 × 10⁵ N/C; along BD: 4 × 10⁵ N/C
solution.why_others_wrong: 2√2 × 10⁵ N/C counts only one charge on each diagonal. Zero would be correct only if all four charges were equal. 8 × 10⁵ N/C adds the four fields as if they were parallel.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electric Charges and Fields', electric field due to a system of charges

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When a positive charge moves in the direction of an electrostatic field, the potential energy of the system decreases.
Statement II: When a negative charge moves opposite to the direction of an electrostatic field, the potential energy of the system increases.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Sign of the change in electrostatic potential energy
solution.explanation: The potential decreases along the field. A change in potential energy is ΔU = qΔV. A positive charge moving along E goes to lower V, so ΔU < 0. A negative charge moving against E goes to higher V (ΔV > 0), and with q < 0 this gives ΔU < 0: its potential energy also decreases, the field doing positive work on it.
steps: Statement I: q > 0, ΔV < 0 → ΔU < 0 → true
Statement II: q < 0, ΔV > 0 → ΔU < 0 (decreases) → false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II forgets that the sign of the charge reverses the sign of ΔU; a negative charge naturally moves against the field, just as a positive one moves along it.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', electrostatic potential and potential energy
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For an isolated point charge, equipotential surfaces drawn for equal steps of potential get farther apart as one moves away from the charge.
Reason (R): The magnitude of the electric field, which equals the rate of fall of potential with distance, decreases with distance from the charge, so a given step of potential needs a larger radial distance.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Spacing of equipotential surfaces
solution.explanation: The equipotentials of a point charge are spheres with V = kq/r. Since |E| = |dV/dr|, the radial gap needed for a fixed ΔV is about ΔV/|E|, which grows as E = kq/r² weakens. For example, with kq = 9 V m the surfaces of 45 V, 30 V and 15 V lie at 0.2 m, 0.3 m and 0.6 m.
steps: E ∝ 1/r² falls with r → Δr grows → A
solution.why_others_wrong: R gives the exact reason for the widening spacing, so it explains A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance', equipotential surfaces and the relation between field and potential
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
